issues.legal_issue: A court should not decide the constitutional validity of a statutory provision on its own initiative when the challenge was not pleaded or properly raised in the proceeding.
material_facts: The dispute reached the High Court in a second appeal concerning a bank’s claim for repayment of an agricultural loan.
The borrower had not challenged the constitutional validity of the statutory exemption in the courts below or before the High Court.
The High Court, on its own initiative, held the exemption unconstitutional under Article 14.

The Supreme Court held that the challenge required specific, clear and unambiguous allegations and that it was inappropriate to decide it in this proceeding. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s finding.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s finding that the exemption was unconstitutional was set aside because the issue had not been properly raised by a party in the proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory provision is presumed constitutional, and the person challenging it must make specific, clear and unambiguous allegations sufficient to show that its classification lacks a rational basis. A court should not decide constitutionality on hypothetical or undeveloped grounds in a proceeding where the challenge was not raised. The Court relied on Harman Singh v. Regional Transport Authority, Sri Venkata Seetaramanjaneya Rice & Oil Mills v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Rajpur Ruda Meha v. State of Gujarat, and Somavanti v. State of Punjab; it also noted the prior decision in Bank of India v. Vijay Transport.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal concerning a civil dispute.
predicates.constitutional_validity_not_pleaded: No party pleaded a challenge to the constitutional validity of the provision in the proceeding.
predicates.high_court_considers_validity_on_its_own: The High Court considered and decided the provision’s validity on its own initiative.

issues.definition: When a second appeal contains no pleaded constitutional challenge and the High Court raises and decides validity on its own, its sua sponte invalidity finding is improper.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory bank is exempt from the agricultural debt-relief law where the law excludes debts owed to corporations formed under special Indian law.
material_facts: A bank created under a statute sued to recover an agricultural loan.
The borrower relied on the agricultural debt-relief law to resist the bank’s claim and recover money through a counterclaim.

The Supreme Court relied on its earlier decision holding that the relevant statutory phrase covered corporations formed by or under a special Indian law, including banks created under the nationalisation law.
After setting aside the unpleaded constitutional ruling, the Supreme Court held that no defence under the agricultural debt-relief law could be raised against the bank’s claim.
issues.conclusion: The agricultural debt-relief law did not provide a defence to the bank’s claim in these proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The exemption for debts owed to a corporation formed in pursuance of a special Indian law includes a corporation formed by or under that law; the law need not have been made by a third party to form the corporation. The Court applied Bank of India v. Vijay Transport, which held that the relevant banking nationalisation law was a special Indian law and that the exemption applied to the bank. Accordingly, the agricultural debt-relief law did not apply to the bank’s loan claim.

rule.if: recovery_suit_by_bank and agricultural_loan_debt and creditor_created_by_special_law and borrower_invokes_agricultural_debt_relief

predicates.recovery_suit_by_bank: A bank brings a proceeding to recover a debt.
predicates.agricultural_loan_debt: The debt arose from a loan made for agricultural purposes.
predicates.creditor_created_by_special_law: The creditor is a corporation formed under a special law.
predicates.borrower_invokes_agricultural_debt_relie: The borrower relies on a law providing relief from agricultural debts to resist recovery.

issues.definition: When a bank created under a special law sues to recover an agricultural loan and the borrower invokes agricultural debt relief, that relief is unavailable as a defence to the bank’s claim.

issues.legal_issue: Where the lower courts have not considered the creditor’s possible defences under the usury law, the unresolved statutory interaction and related questions of excessive interest must be considered on remand, with an opportunity to rebut any applicable presumption.
material_facts: The trial and first appellate courts decided the dispute principally under the agricultural debt-relief law and did not examine the applicability of the usury law or possible relief under it.
The High Court did not properly examine the interaction between the usury law and the banking-law provision restricting courts from reopening bank transactions on the ground of interest rates.
The record did not address whether a presumption of excessive interest would arise if the usury law applied, or whether the bank could rebut that presumption.
The Supreme Court remitted the second appeal for consideration of those matters and permitted the borrower to raise additional grounds.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court made no ruling on the merits of the usury-law issues and remitted them to the High Court for consideration, including whether the bank could rebut any applicable presumption of excessive interest.
issues.legal_principle: The interaction between the provision restricting courts from reopening bank transactions on the ground of interest rates and the Usurious Loans Act, 1918, required consideration because the lower courts had not addressed it. If the Usurious Loans Act applied and its presumption under the proviso to Section 3(2)(b) arose, the bank had to have an opportunity to rebut that presumption. The Court left these questions, and any other legal impediments to charging compound interest on agricultural advances, for the High Court to consider on remand.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal concerning a creditor’s claim for repayment.
predicates.lower_courts_did_not_examine_usury_defen: The lower courts decided the dispute on another ground and did not examine whether the creditor could obtain relief under the law addressing excessive loans.
predicates.applicability_of_usury_law_remains_unres: Whether that law applies, and whether a presumption of excessive interest can be rebutted, remains undecided.

issues.definition: When a second appeal reaches the court after the lower courts have left the usury defence and its applicability unresolved, those issues are remanded for consideration.
